newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's rate cut outlook blurs as EMU nears.
newsitem.headline: Spain's rate cut outlook blurs as EMU nears.

text.p: The Bank of Spain's next cut in interest rates will be a highly sensitive decision, hinging on Spain's prospects for entry into the first round of monetary union, economists said.
Some see the cuts as a reflection of economic fundamentals. As these continue to improve, assuring Spain's EMU entry, more rates cuts will indeed come through, they say.
Economy Secretary Cristobal Montoro said on Friday that the central bank would continue to cut interest rates if the downtrend in inflation and the deficit continued.
"As inflation and the public deficit confirm their downtrend, we will certainly see further cuts in interest rates," Montoro said.

But given the central bank's much-vaunted caution, some economists consider that Friday's 25 basis point key rate cut to 5.75 percent may be the central bank's penultimate or even its last move because the markets' monetary union jitters will put the bank on hold.
"Maybe we'll see another 25 basis point cut in the next three months, (but) it'll be the only one for a long, long while," Jose Luis Alzola, Salomon Brothers economist told RFTV.
"The Bank of Spain will be cautious after that (second rate cut), it will depend on how European (monetary) union proceeds," he added.

The rate-cutting cycle began at the end of 1995, when the central bank sliced 25 basis points off its key rate to leave it at 9.00 percent. This was followed by a total of seven cuts in 1996, leaving the rate at 6.25 percent in December.
Another economist, surprised by today's move, was not optimistic about Friday's cut, or the possibilities of more.
"I was surprised because it seems to me it is based only on good February CPI, shrugging off other things such as the peseta's weakness," said Gregorio Gomez, an economist at an unnamed brokerage.
"It could be the last time they cut," he added.
But others say the Bank of Spain has considerably more room to cut based on improving fundamentals.

February inflation data provided a pleasant surprise on Thursday, with the month to month Consumer Price Index (CPI) unexpectedly falling 0.1 percent from January for a 2.5 percent year on year inflation rate.
That figure, down from 2.9 percent last month, is the lowest Spain has seen for 28 years, and very near to December's 2.6 percent target. This inspired today's cut, analysts said.
The decision was controversial for some in that currency stability is a key factor for entry into monetary union, and the peseta has been somewhat volatile recently.
But it is not so weak that it would deter the central bank from cutting, now or in the future, some argue.
"The current peseta level didn't stop the cut because we can't say the peseta is weak at levels of between 84.85/85.00 to the mark," said Alfredo Urrutia, economist at Societe Generale.
Carmen Hernansanz at Merrill Lynch Espana agreed.

"The peseta has gone through episodes of volatility. But this doesn't mean that (the central bank) won't carry on cutting, as inflation will continue to decline and the Bank of Spain could cut again in May or even before, depending on new improvements in CPI."
Inflation and monetary union considerations are the key focuses for the central bank in this crucial year. And fluctuations in the markets cannot be ignored, no matter how much inflation improves.

"(The central bank) had economic reasons to cut even more, at around 50 basis points, but at the same time EMU jitters and peseta weakness were suggesting they hold rates. So they cut 25 basis points which is neutral," Juan Mielgo, economist at Bank of America in Madrid said.
If the move responds to an improved inflation outlook, combined with a prudent stance regarding the future, so much the better for the financial markets, Hernansanz said.
"I think the Bank of Spain has earned its reputation with caution so, if it cuts rates, it's because it is reasonably satisfied with prices and this generates confidence in the markets," she added.
